prize_parts.citation: For the invention of the magic-wavelength optical lattice clock and its development into the most accurate and stable frequency standard, with systematic uncertainty at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep B012 as a single-part prize to Katori and Ye, and my configuration has not changed since round 1. Having read the full exchange, the case rests on what I ask of any experimental result: it must be reproduced independently, the systematics must be understood, and the credited contribution must have been decisive. The lattice clock meets all three. Katori's magic-wavelength condition is the enabling idea that lets thousands of neutral atoms be interrogated with Doppler and recoil shifts removed. Ye's group then took the clock to record accuracy and stability, and JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE and NPL now compare such clocks at about 1e-18. The result is a measured number, not an interpretation, so it will not be revised by later theory. It also opens real measurements: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, tests of constant drift, dark-matter searches and a likely redefinition of the second. The credit is the cleanest on the shortlist, since all six members who ranked it proposed the same two names. On the chair's question about the 2005 and 2012 prizes, I think a citation built around the magic-wavelength lattice and its realisation as an optical frequency standard separates this work from the comb and from single-ion control. The overlap objection would become decisive only if the citation described clocks or precision metrology in general terms. That is a drafting question, and I think it can be solved.
statement.case_against: My strongest reservation is unchanged: a third prize in the precision-metrology neighbourhood after 2005 and 2012 can be read as incremental, and Katori and Ye stand on the comb and on ion-clock work. Early lattice-clock contributors (Lemonde, Pal'chikov, Takamoto, Ludlow) are not covered by two names, and the committee should say plainly in its record why they are not credited. The SI second has not been redefined, so a sceptic can say the payoff is still pending. I also hold this view as a non-specialist in atomic physics. I am relying on Lindroth, Kroll and Olsson for priority and for how decisive Ye's contribution is, and I should not hide that dependence behind the count of five round-1 supporters. That count is not a scientific argument, and I do not treat it as one. B042 has the opposite problem. It is scientifically exciting, but the pairing mechanism and the nature of the correlated insulators are still debated, twist-angle disorder limits reproducibility, and the experimental credit leaves out Yuan Cao and several follow-up groups.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B012 first as precision atomic physics, attributes the magic-wavelength idea to Katori and the record accuracy and stability to Ye, and asks colleagues from other fields to test her view because she may over-weight her own area.
responses.response: I take up that invitation from the instrument side. The cross-laboratory comparisons at 1e-18, including fibre links, are the kind of independent check that would convince me in my own field, and they do not depend on a specialist's taste. I also accept your attribution: the lattice idea is Katori's and the performance record is Ye's. My remaining question is the one in the chair's summary. Is Ye's role limited to the Sr clock, or does the many-body clock and the frequency-comb link make him central rather than a convenient second name? If you can say that the pair would be the first two names in any atomic-physics committee, I will treat the credit as settled for my purposes.

responses.point: Kroll describes the lattice clock as a new measurement technique with quantitative, repeated evidence, and asks whether the first lattice-clock demonstrations and Ye's many-body clock work should be described separately in the citation.
responses.response: I agree that the evidence is the strong point, and I think his question is the right test of the wording. I would keep one citation part and not split the credit. Katori is credited for the invention of the lattice clock and Ye for taking it to the accuracy and stability that makes it a standard. This avoids implying that the many-body work is a separate prize-worthy discovery, and it leaves room to say in the record that Takamoto, Ludlow and Lemonde did important early demonstrations. A two-part prize would not fit the three-person limit anyway. If you think a priority claim outside the pair is strong enough to displace Ye, please say so plainly now, because that is the point that would change my position.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers B042 as a clean prediction followed by a decisive experimental clue, reports eight of eight members ranking it, and says he would not be embarrassed if the committee chose B012.
responses.response: I agree that prediction followed by experiment is a strong pattern, and I am glad B012 is acceptable to you. I would not accept that universal ranking means it is the more settled choice. It was ranked by everyone, but five members rank it below B012 and only three place it first. On maturity I part from you: the superconducting mechanism is still open, and you list it yourself as the main risk of a hasty prize. For B042, what would move me is evidence that the correlated phases, and in particular the superconductivity, have been reproduced across devices in a way that controls twist-angle disorder, and an agreed split of the experimental credit. Without those I rank it second, not first.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B042 as theory delivering a quantitative prediction and nature delivering a new quantum state, but concedes that optical lattice clocks would be a safer, more mature topic, and asks whether the superconducting mechanism is part of the discovery.
responses.response: I think the mechanism is a follow-up question if the citation is confined to flat bands and the observation of correlated insulating and superconducting states, as Danielsson's wording is. But the prize would then stand on the observation. Reproducibility across independent groups is the right test, and you list twist-angle disorder as a concern. I also take your point that B012 is the safer choice and you accept it as an alternative. The question I would put to B042 supporters is whether the three-name limit really lets the experimental half of the credit stand with Jarillo-Herrero alone, when Cao was first author. That question is cleaner for B012.

responses.point: Olsson regards the magic-wavelength lattice as a distinct original invention and the measured performance as not a matter of interpretation, and she does not find the overlap with 2005 and 2012 or the pending redefinition of the second decisive.
responses.response: I agree on both. On the redefinition of the second, I would treat it as a consequence of the discovery and not as a precondition. The Nobel Prize has not waited for a standards body in other metrology-related awards, and the independent comparisons at 1e-18 are what any redefinition rests on. Waiting would also mean the committee honours the standard-setting decision and not the physics. I would not be dogmatic if the committee preferred another year, but I would want the reason to be a specific missing result and not the calendar.

uncertainties: Whether Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow or Pal'chikov have a priority claim strong enough to displace or add to Katori and Ye, and whether Ye's role is central enough. I rely on Lindroth, Kroll and Olsson for this and cannot verify it myself.
Whether the committee accepts the distinction from the 2005 and 2012 prizes once the citation is tied to the magic-wavelength lattice, or whether a sceptic would still see a third metrology prize.
Whether the redefinition of the second should be treated as a consequence rather than a precondition. I hold it as a consequence but not firmly.
Whether B042 will look more mature in a year or two, once the pairing mechanism and credit split are clearer. That could change the order in a later year, but I do not see it changing the choice now.
My knowledge of IceCube and GRB-afterglow history is from memory and I have not verified it.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for B012, and I have no tie to Katori or Ye. My membership in PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur and my gamma-ray polarimetry plans put me in the same field as B035 (IceCube) and B016 (GRB afterglows). B035 is listed only as an alternative, and as Chair I would step back from a decision on either if it became the leading candidate. I have no tie to B042 or its credited names.
